INTEREST OF AMICUS CURIAE 1
The Electronic Privacy Information Center (EPIC)
is a public-interest research center in Washington, D.C.,
established in 1994 to secure the fundamental right to
privacy in the digital age for all people. Central to that
work is oversight of how government agencies collect,
use, retain, and share personal information.
EPIC has long worked to protect voter privacy and
regularly participates as amicus curiae in cases
concerning it. See, e.g., Br. of Amici Curiae EPIC et al.,
Crawford v. Marion Cnty. Election Bd. , 553 U.S. 181
(2008) (No. 07-21); Br. of Amicus Curiae EPIC, Pub. Int.
Legal Found., Inc. v. Bellows, 92 F.4th 36 (1st Cir. 2024)
(No. 23-1361); Br. of Amicus Curiae EPIC, Veasey v.
Abbott, 830 F.3d 216 (5th Cir. 2016) (en banc) (No. 14-
41127). EPIC has also engaged directly with the recent
modifications to the Systematic Alien Verification for
Entitlements (SAVE) program. In December 2025, it led
a coalition in submitting comments to the Social Security
Administration (SSA) and the Department of Homeland
Security (DHS) on the computer matching agreements
and sys tem-of-records notices in connection with the
modifications DHS made to the SAVE program in 2025,
which integrated SSA databases into the program a nd
introduced a bulk-search capability to allow state and
local officials to upload entire voter files and conduct
citizenship checks of registered voters .

1 No counsel for any party authored this brief in whole or in part,
and no entity or person, aside from amicus curiae, its members, or
its counsel, made a monetary contribution intended to fund the
preparation or submission of this brief.

2

EPIC is a plaintiff in League of Women Voters v.
DHS, 835 F. Supp. 3d 79 (D.D.C.), stay granted, No.
26A308, 2026 WL 2879700 (U.S. Sep. 25, 2026) (per
curiam), a challenge to those modifications. In that case,
EPIC reviewed the administrative records of DHS and
SSA for modified SAVE and helped develop the factual
record on how the system works and how it affects
voters. EPIC submits this brief to describe that record,
which bears on the second question presented as to
whether the 90-day provision of the National Voter
Registration Act (NVRA) applies to Arizona’s SAVE-
based voter-registration cancellation program.
SUMMARY OF ARGUMENT
The United States defends Arizona’s SAVE-based
voter-registration cancellation program on the premise
that noncitizens identified by the program —like voters
who have died, have been convicted of certain crimes, or
have been adjudicated mentally incapacitated —are
ineligible voters who may be removed from the rolls in
the 90 days before a federal election because their legal
status is “readily ascertainable.” Br. for the United
States as Resp’t Supporting Pet’r 42 [hereinafter “U.S.
Br.”]. That is because, according to the United States,
SAVE is “a single, reliable source for verifying noncitizen status nationwide.” 2 That premise is false. SAVE
routinely misidentifies citizens as noncitizens, and those
errors cannot reliably be corrected in the weeks before
an election. Application of the 90-day quiet period under

2 Press Release, DHS, DHS, USCIS, DOGE Overhaul Systemat i c
Alien Verification for Entitlements Database (Apr. 22, 2025).

3

the NVRA is critical to prevent the erroneous removal
of eligible voters.
I. Arizona law  requires each county recorder to
compare against SAVE, every month, all registran ts
who have not provided documentary proof of citizenship.
Ariz. Rev. Stat. § 16-165(I). Since SAVE’s modification
in 2025, c ounty recorders can upload their entire voter
files to SAVE in bulk, and SAVE then attempts to
match voters’ names, dates of birth, and Social Security
numbers against SSA records. DHS v. League of Women
Voters, No. 26A308, 2026 WL 2879700, at *1 (U.S . Sep.
25, 2026) (per curiam) [hereinafter “Stay Op.”] . The
result is a systematic program that screens whole
categories of voters against federal data on a fixed
schedule. As the G overnment acknowledges, that
program “is not time -limited,” and it continues during
“the 90-day period before a federal election.” U.S. Br. 10.
II. No party to this case  contests the system atic
nature of Arizona’s program. A program that runs
categories of registrants through a database each mon th
is undoubtedly “systematic” under the NVRA.  As the
Eleventh Circuit explained, such a program does not
“rely upon individualized information or investigation to
determine which names from the voter registry to
remove.” Arcia v. Fla. Sec’y of State, 772 F.3d 1335, 1344
(11th Cir. 2014). It uses “a mass computerized datamatching process.” Id. Arizona’s own Elections
Procedures Manual  classifies periodic noncitizenship
cancellations based on jury reports and motor -vehicle
records as “systematic.” Ariz. Sec’y of State, 2025
Elections Procedures Manual  53 (Dec. 2025)
[hereinafter “Manual”] . Because it is systematic,

4

Arizona’s program therefore may not run during the
NVRA’s 90-day quiet period provision unless, as the
Government contends, Congress meant to leav e
removals based on citizenship status outside that period.
III. A SAVE-based removal is not the kind of
removal that Congress meant to exempt from the quiet
period. A SAVE-based identification of alleged
noncitizens is an inference from a database match
against SSA citizenship data, which individuals have “no
obligation” to update after they naturalize. Joint
Appendix, League of Women Voters v. DHS, No. 1:25-cv-
03501 (D.D.C. June 12, 2026), Dkt.  110, at SSA -AR-44
[hereinafter “SSA -AR”]. DHS’s own privacy
assessments warn that shortfalls in that data “could
cause incomplete or false results.” Id.  at DHS-AR-260,
302 [hereinafter “DHS -AR”]. The experience of States
and counties confirms the warning. In Maricopa County,
Arizona, 52 of 60 voters flagged by SAVE and
investigated by the county attorney turned out to be
citizens, and in Texas, citizenship was later proven for at
least 506 of the 2,724 voters that SAVE flagged. By
contrast , the statuses Congress exempted from the
NVRA quiet period—d eath, conviction of a crime, and
adjudicated incapacity—are documented events or
judgments about an identified person based on official
records that are regularly transmitted to election
officials.
IV. Applying the NVRA’s 90 -day quiet period to
SAVE-based removal programs is critical because their
errors cannot be corrected quickly. Citizens wrongly
flagged by SAVE often have to wait weeks to correct
federal records or obtain documentary proof of

5

citizenship. That burden falls on citizens who have done
nothing wrong, and in Arizona , a notice that goes
unanswered leads to cancellation of the voter’ s
registration and referral to prosecutors.  Moreover, the
remedies the G overnment offers come too late. A suit
under Section 11(b) of the NVRA requires notice and a
waiting period, and in practice depends on a voter
finding counsel able to sue and obtain relief in a very
short time . And the ability to cast a provisional ballot
offers no help  in Arizona because a ballot cast by a
cancelled voter is not counted. Finally, a pplying the
quiet period to SAVE-based programs does not leav e
States without recourse. They remain free to check
citizenship at registration and to act on individualized
information at any time. What the quiet period bars is a
mass, mechanical removal program like Arizona’s in the
weeks when its errors cannot be fixed.
ARGUMENT
I. H.B. 2243  REQUIRES MONTHLY CHECKS AGA I NST
SAVE.
Arizona law requires election officials to compare th e
State’s voter rolls periodically against several
databases. Ariz. Rev. Stat. § 16-165(G) –(K). One is “the
systematic alien verification for entitlements program
maintained by the United States citizenship and
immigration services,” or SAVE. Id. § 16-165(I). Each
month, when “practicable,” county recorders must use
SAVE “to verify the citizenship status” of registered
voters who have not submitted documentary proof of
citizenship. Id.

6

When a recorder “obtains information pursuant to
this section and confirms that the person registered is
not a United States citizen,” the recorder must mail the
voter a notice that his or her  registration “will be
canceled in thirty-five days unless the person provides
satisfactory evidence of United States citizenship.” Id.
§ 16-165(A)(10). If the voter does not respond in time,
“the county recorder shall cancel the registration and
notify the county attorney and attorney general for
possible investigation.” Id. As the United States
acknowledges, the program “is not time -limited.” U.S.
Br. 10.  Officials continue to act on it “during the 90 -day
period before a federal election.” Id .
Arizona’s Attorney General has advised that
identification by SAVE “can, in some situations, provid e
evidence that a person is not a U.S. citizen” sufficient to
trigger the cancellation  process. Ariz. Att’y Gen. Op.
I25-007, at 21 (2025). The statute does not define how the
recorder otherwise “confirms that the person registered
is not a United States citizen”  before sending the
cancellation notice. Ariz. Rev. Stat. § 16-165(A)(10). In
practice, a cancellation notice often  follows a routine
database search.
Until 2025, citizenship checks under SAVE had a
narrow reach.  Users had to search one person at a time
by a DHS numeric identifier, and SAVE held records on
U.S.-born citizens only if they had some other
interaction with DHS , had applied for government
benefits or licenses, or had been subject to certain
background checks . League of Women Voters, 835 F.
Supp. 3d at 102; DHS -AR-111, 247– 48. Even so, the
Eleventh Circuit held that a Florida program relying on

7

that older version of SAVE was a “systematic” removal
program subject to the quiet period. Arcia , 772 F.3d at
1339– 40, 1344.
In 2025, DHS changed SAVE in “two key respects.”
Stay Op., 2026 WL 2879700, at *1. It allowed users “to
conduct bulk searches of multiple individuals at once,”
id., by uploading a file of voters’ names, dates of birth,
and full or partial Social Security numbers, League of
Women Voters v. DHS , No. 26 -5243, 2026 WL 2643439,
at *2 (D.C. Cir. Sep. 4, 2026) (per curiam) , stay granted,
No. 26A308, 2026 WL 2879700 (U.S. Sep. 25, 2026) (per
curiam). And it linked SAVE to SSA records, extending
its reach to “easily over 300 million” people, including
U.S.-born citizens. SSA -AR-238; League of Women
Voters, 835 F. Supp. 3d at 103. Thus, while under the old
system, § 16-165(I)’s monthly checks could reach only
registrants with a DHS identifier —which in practice
meant naturalized citizens and noncitizens , Pet. App.
41a—now they can reach any registrant with a Social
Security number.
II. ARIZONA ’S MONTHLY SAVE CHECKS ARE A
“SYSTEM ATIC” REMOVAL PROGRAM .
No party to this case contests that Arizona’s monthly
SAVE checks are systematic. Indeed, the name of the
database alone—the Systematic Alien Verification for
Entitlements program—reveals its nature.
Arizona law requires county recorders to run
categories of registered voters through SAVE each
month, comparing registrants against SAVE to verify
their citizenship status, Ariz. Rev. Stat. §  16-165(I), th e
“purpose of which is to systematically remove the names

8

of ineligible voters from the official lists of eligible
voters,” 52 U.S.C. §  20507(c)(2)(A) . The program
compares registered voters against a federal database
on a fixed schedule. Its principal category, every voter
registered without documentary proof of citizenship, is
defined by registration status alone , with no
individualized consideration.
In Arizona, county recorders are the designated
SAVE users, see DHS-AR-528, and their part of the
process is automated from start to finish.  The recorder
fills a spreadsheet template with each voter’s name, date
of birth, Social Security number, and the purpose of the
query (for example, voter verification) , and uploads it.
League of Women Voters, 835 F. Supp. 3d at 103; DHS -
AR-1443– 44. SAVE then “automatically discloses the
voters’ uploaded data to SSA,” and SSA “automatically
discloses” its search results back to DHS. League of
Women Voters, 835 F. Supp. 3d at 103.  As the court
below put it, the statute obtains its information “through
the systematic comparison of all —or groups of —
registered voters to various databases,” and the
cancellation that follows is “[c]ancellation of batches of
registered voters based on a s et procedure.” Pet. App.
45a. That is the same “mass computerized data-matching
process to compare the voter rolls with other state and
federal databases” the Eleventh Circuit held systematic
in Arcia, 772 F.3d at 1344. The notice  that a flagged
voter receives comes “only after the systematic
comparison prompts the mailing, as opposed to it being
prompted by an individualized investigation.” Pet. App.
45a.

9

States and localities have used these bulk uploads at
scale. By October 2025, Texas had compared its entire
list of registered voters against SAVE data. Decl. of
Christopher Davis ¶ 5, League of Women Voters v. DHS,
No. 1:25-cv -03501 (D.D.C. Mar. 20, 2026), Dkt.  68-1
[hereinafter “Davis Decl.”]; see id.  Ex. D (more than 18
million records). In 2026, Yavapai County, Arizona , ran
every active and inactive voter with a Social Security
number on file through SAVE—187,719 in all.3 Between
January 2025 and April 2026, SAVE processed 59.7
million voter verification queries, with  some users
submitting bulk requests “relating to millions of
individuals at one time.” Decl. of Brian Broderick
¶¶ 18(b), 22, League of Women Voters, No. 1:25-cv-03501
(D.D.C. Apr. 2, 2026), Dkt.  77-2 [hereinafter “Broderick
Decl.”].
Jurisdictions likewise use systematic notification
forms following a SAVE check. For example, after
Texas ran its full voter roll through SAVE, its counties
sent flagged voters letters containing the sam e
sentence: SAVE records “show that you were not a
United States citizen at the time of the comparativ e
process.” Decl. of Anthony Nel ¶ 13, League of Women
Voters, No. 1:25 -cv-03501 (D.D.C. Mar. 12, 2026) , Dkt.
66-3 [hereinafter “Nel Decl.”]; Decl. of Cory Doe ¶  13,
id., Dkt. 66-6 [hereinafter “Cory Doe Decl.”].  And
Arizona uses similar boilerplate language to reject th ose
applying for voter registration. See  Manual 341 (“[W]e
were unable to match the immigration/citizenship
number you provided with U.S. Department of

3 Michelle M. Burchill, Yavapai Cnty. Recorder, My Experience
Using the SAVE Database 3 (2026).

10

Homeland Security records.”); see id . at 343 (same).
Arizona’s SAVE-based removal program is thus
systematic from start to finish.
III. A SAVE NONCITIZEN IDENTIFICATION  IS NOT A
“READILY ASCERTAINABLE ” STATUS LIKE
CONVICTION , ADJUDICATED INCAPACITY , OR
DEATH.
In enacting the N VRA, Congress expressly
exempted from the quiet period removals based on a
registered voter’s criminal conviction, adjudicated
mental incapacity under state law, or death . 52 U.S.C. §
20507(c)(2).  The Government contends that
noncitizenship status —like conviction, mental
incapacity, and death—is “readily ascertainable. ” U.S.
Br. 41-42. That is false. No single agency—at the federal
or state level —has a comprehensive dataset capable of
providing accurate, real -time verification of individuals’
U.S. citizenship status. Instead, federal agencies possess
citizenship data collected for disparate, congressio nally
authorized functions, but which was never meant to be
fed into a centralized database. And to the extent local
officials in States like Arizona have citizenship data at
all, it is even less complete and more diffuse .
The SAVE database is no exception. SSA r ecords
disclosed through SAVE were collected for SSA’s own
program purposes concerning work authorization and
eligibility for SSA benefits—not citizenship verification
or election administration . See SSA-AR-115– 16, 132,
149, 168– 69, 188– 89, 207. 4 Arizona county recorders’

4See also SSA, Program Operations Manual System (POMS), GN

11

reliance on SAVE for list maintenance thus risks
disenfranchising lawfully registered voters if recorders
may remove purported noncitizens during the quiet
period.
A. The Government Has Repeatedly Admitted
that SAVE’s Citizenship Data Is Incomplete
and Unreliable.
Since DHS modified SAVE  in 2025, it has conceded
that, due to “shortfalls in data accuracy,” the system
cannot reliably confirm citizenship for citizens born
outside the United States (e.g., naturalized, derived, and
acquired citizens). 5 See DHS-AR-260, 277, 302 (DHS
“Privacy Threshold Analysis” documents finding that
“[s]hortfalls in data accuracy in the system could cause
incomplete or false results”). This is because, among
other reasons, the United States is home to nearly 25
million naturalized citizens, 6 and year over year, that

00303.000 Citizenship, Alien Status and Residency (Jan. 9, 2026) ,
https://perma.cc/R7CE-W26P; 20 C.F.R. § 422.104 (section titled
“Who can be assigned a social security number”);  id. § 422. 107
(section titled “Evidence requirements”).
5 Acquired citizenship is “[c]itizenship conferred at birth on children
born abroad to a U.S. citizen parent(s).” USCIS, Acquired
citizenship, Glossary of Terms. Derived citizenship is “[c]itizenship
conveyed to children through the naturalization of their parents or,
under certain circumstances, to foreign-born children adopted by
U.S. citizen parents.” USCIS, Derivative citizenship, Glossary of
Terms.
6 U.S. Census Bureau, Nativity and Citizenship Status in the
United States, Am. Cmty. Surv. 1 -Year Estimates, tbl. B05001
(2023).

12

number grows by the hundreds of thousands. 7
Citizenship data housed at SSA and incorporated in
SAVE reflects a person’s citizenship status only at the
time they applied for a S ocial Security number ; that
status does not automatically update if the person later
naturalizes or derives citizenship from a parent’s
naturalization, nor must such an individual report a
change in citizenship status unless applying for SSA
benefits. SSA-AR-44, 103.
Thus, a naturalized citizen who applied for a Social
Security card or otherwise interacted with SSA before
naturalization may be incorrectly identified as a
noncitizen in SSA records. SSA itself has repeatedly
recognized the dangers of incorporating its stale
citizenship data into SAVE, noting that “citizenship
information in SSA’s records might not be current,”
SSA-AR-44, and, as a result, its “citizenship information
is accurate for SSA’s program purposes” only; “if used
later for other purposes, it may not be current” becau se
“SSA is not the custodian of U.S. citizenship records.”
SSA-AR-103. 8
Similarly, if an acquired or derived citizen has not
obtained a “certificate of United States citizenship” from
DHS—which “frequently” is the case, DHS -AR-259—

IV.  THE QUIET PERIOD PROTECTS CITIZENS FROM
SAVE ERRORS THAT CANNOT BE CORRECT ED
BEFORE AN ELECTION .
The Government contends that applying the quiet
period to noncitizen removals buys little and costs much.
It says that systematic checks are the only way to catch
noncitizens who register late, and that a citizen remov ed
in error can sue under Section 11(b) of the NVRA. U.S.
Br. 42 –43. Each argument assumes that a SAVE error
can be found and fixed quickly. DHS’s own procedures,

21

and the experience of the States and counties that have
used SAVE, show that it cannot .
A. A SAVE Error Cannot Reliably Be Corrected
in the Weeks Before an Election.
Application of the 90-day quiet period to SAVE -
based identifications of alleged noncitizens is critical
because there is a high risk that eligible voters
incorrectly identified as noncitizens will not be able to
correct the error in the short time before the election .
The Eleventh Circuit has explained why the NVRA
treats the final three months before a federal election
differently. At most points in the election cycle, “eligible
voters who are incorrectly removed have enough time to
rectify any errors.” Arcia, 772 F.3d at 1346. But
“[e]ligible voters removed days or weeks before Election
Day will likely not be able to correct the State’s errors
in time to vote.” Id. That is why the NVRA “permits
systematic removal programs at any time except for the
90 days before an election because that is when the risk
of disfranchising eligible voters is the greatest.” Id.
SSA answers a SAVE query “within one second or
less.” SSA-AR-42. Correcting a stale record can take far
longer. A Virginia voter received a Social Security
number in 1987, naturalized in 1995, and still appeared in
SSA’s records as a noncitizen in 2025. When the voter
called to fix the error, the earliest in-person appointment
available was November 24, 2025, twenty days after th e
State’s election. Decl. of J. Doe 6 ¶¶ 2, 6, 9, 15, 19, League
of Women Voters, No. 1:25 -cv-03501 (D.D.C. Oct. 7,
2025),  Dkt. 16-8. A Texan who obtained his number as a
permanent resident later became a citizen through his
parents’ naturalization. A county letter gave him 30 days

22

to prove his U.S. citizenship . His only proof was an
expired passport. He applied to renew it, but the county
cancelled his registration before the new passport
arrived. Nel Decl. ¶¶ 4– 5, 12– 14, 17, 22, 25.
Counties need time as well. On October 16, 2025,
Texas placed 97 SAVE matches in Travis County’s
online repository. The county learned of the list five days
later. Davis Decl. ¶¶ 6–7, 9. Between then and December
17, its voter registration director sought state record s to
evaluate the matches —an effort that took “an untold
number of hours of work.”  Id. ¶¶ 10 –18. In Maricopa
County, it took the county attorney’s office six months
to determine that 52 of 60 voters flagged as noncitizen s
were in fact citizens. See supra Part III.B.  And not all
counties can or will dedicate the time and resources
expended by Travis County—home to Austin —and
Maricopa County—home to Phoenix.
B. The Burden of a SAVE Error Falls on Citizens
Who Have Done Nothing Wrong.
SAVE’s errors fall most heavily on citizens whose
status changed after they last dealt with SSA, such as
naturalized and derived citizens. See supra Part III.A.
The record shows SAVE flagging even citizens who hold
passports. Two Texas voters who acquired citizenship
through their parents had been issued U.S. passports in
2012 and 2013, yet each received a county letter stating
that SAVE records showed they “were not a United
States citizen.” Nel Decl. ¶¶ 5 –6, 13; Cory Doe Decl.
¶¶ 5–6, 13. Having to prove one’s citizenship in respon se
is itself a burden, as this Court recognized in granting
the Government’s stay application. A naturalized citizen
whose SSA record was out of date “likely would have

23

been required to provide additional proof of citizenship,”
and the “need to take . . . affirmative steps to avoid risk
of harm . . . constitutes a cognizable injury.” Stay Op. ,
2026 WL 2879700, at *2 (quoting Meese v. Keene, 481
U.S. 465, 475 (1987)  (ellipsis in original)).
The notices that start the cancellation  clock can be
easy to miss. Texas counties sent form letters stating
that a “comparison of the information in your voter
registration records with the United States Citizenship
and Immigration Services SAVE records show that you
were not a United States citizen at the time of the
comparative process.” Nel Decl. ¶ 13; Cory Doe Decl.
¶ 13. The envelopes had no markings showing that they
concerned the voter’s registration. Nel Decl. ¶ 15; Cory
Doe Decl. ¶ 15. One voter set the letter aside because it
“looked like junk mail, or even a scam,” and had a week
left to respond when the letter was finally opened. Decl.
of Alex Doe ¶¶ 12– 13, League of Women Voters, No.
1:25-cv-03501 (D.D.C. Mar. 12, 2026) , Dkt. 66-4
[hereinafter “Alex Doe Decl.”] . Arizona’s Attorney
General has recognized the same problem, noting that a
voter may fail to respond because of “not seeing the
request, not fully understanding the request, or perhaps
even suspecting that the request is not genuinely from
the same government office.” Ariz. Att’y Gen. Op. I25-
007, at 23.
Some voters never receive the notice at all. Bailey
Doe naturalized in 2021 and holds both a certificate of
naturalization and a passport. Decl. of Bailey Doe ¶¶ 5–
7, League of Women Voters, No. 1:25 -cv-03501 (D.D.C.
Mar. 12, 2026) , Dkt. 66-5 [hereinafter “Bailey Doe
Decl.”]. After voting in November 2025, Bailey Doe

24

received a notice dated in mid -December stating that
her registration had been cancelled for failure to respond
to a “Notice of Examination.” She never received that
notice. Id. ¶¶ 11–14. It took three telephone calls to learn
that the cancellation rested on a SAVE identification ,
and the county had no record of mailing the earlier
notice. Id. ¶¶ 20 –22. The registration “remained
cancelled during the voting period for the March 3, 2026
primary election in Texas,” and Bailey Doe “was unable
to vote.” Id.  ¶ 31. The cancellation notice was dated
within 90 days of that primary.
Voters in under -resourced counties are particularly
at risk for disenfranchisement. Travis County’s voter
registration director warned that wrongly flagged
voters in counties without the resources to investigate
“may be removed from the voter rolls improperly and
very likely will not realize the removal until they go to
the polls to vote.” Davis Decl. ¶ 20.  And the
consequences can reach beyond the registration. Under
Arizona’s statute, if a flagged voter does not respond
within 35 days, “the county recorder shall cancel the
registration and notify the county attorney and attorney
general for possible investigation.” Ariz. Rev. Stat. § 16-
165(A)(10). Accordingly, a citizen could be not just
disenfranchised, but also the target of a criminal

C. The Remedies the Government Offers Arrive
Too Late.
The Government suggests that there is no problem
here because a person wrongly removed from the voter
rolls by a SAVE misidentification has an available

25

remedy—a private suit  under Section 11(b) of the
NVRA, which the Government says “is expressly made
available even within the 90-day window before a federal
election.” U.S. Br. 43. But under Section 11(b), a  person
aggrieved must notify the State’s chief election official
and wait 90 days for a cure. The wait is 20 days if the
violation occur s within 120 days of a federal election. 52
U.S.C. § 20510(b)(1)–(2). Notice is excused only when the
violation occurs within 30 days of the election. Id.
§ 20510(b)(3). A ccordingly, a citizen cancelled during the
quiet period must learn of the cancellation, give notice,
wait, sue, and win an injunction—all before Election
Day.
Even organized plaintiffs with counsel already in
place have struggled to obtain timely relief. In Virginia,
plaintiffs sued “on the first day they could do so without
waiting another 20 days” and won a preliminary
injunction 11 days before the 2024 election, but this
Court stayed it five days later. Va. Coal. for Immigrant
Rights v. Beals, No. 24-2071, 2024 WL 4601052, at *2 (4th
Cir. Oct. 27, 2024) , stay granted, No. 24A407, 2024 WL
4608863 (U.S. Oct. 30, 2024) ; Va. Coal. for Immigrant
Rights v. Beals, 803 F. Supp. 3d 454, 463 (E.D. Va. 2025);
Beals v. Va. Coal. for Immigrant Rights , No. 24A407,
2024 WL 4608863 (U.S. Oct. 30, 2024). In Alabama, relief
came less than three weeks before the same election, an d
only after the Secretary of State “admitted that his
purge list included thousands of United States citizens.”
Ala. Coal. for Immigrant Justice v. Allen , No. 2:24 -cv-
1254, 2024 WL 4510476, at *1–2 (N.D. Ala. Oct. 16, 2024).
The Government also points to NVRA Section
8(b)(1), which requires that list maintenance be

26

“uniform, nondiscriminatory, and in compliance with the
Voting Rights Act.” 52 U.S.C. § 20507(b)(1) . In its view,
that requirement “sets a modest floor” for noncitizen
removal programs. U.S. Br. 43. But Section 8(b)(1)
governs how a program operates. It does not say wh en a
program may run, and a voter can enforce it only
through the same Section 11(b) suit. This case shows
how slowly that process works. Arizona enacted H.B.
2243 in 2022, and only in 2025 did the Ninth Circuit hold
that its citizenship checks violate NVRA Section 8(b)(1)
because they are “likely to have a discriminatory impact
on [naturalized] citizens.” Pet. App. 40a‒ 41a. That
holding is not before this Court.
Nor would a provisional ballot help a citizen whose
voter registration was cancelled under § 16-165(A)(10).
Arizona counts a provisional ballot only if the record er
confirms “that the voter was registered to vote and was
eligible to vote in the election.” Manual 239; see A riz.
Rev. S tat. §  16-584(E). For a cancelled voter, the
provisional affidavit can serve only as a registration “for
future elections (not the current election the provisional
ballot was used for).” Manual 240. And a registration
counts for an election only if received “bef ore midnight
of the twenty -ninth day preceding the date of the
election.” Ariz. Rev. Stat. § 16-120(A).
D. States Can Keep Noncitizens Off Their Voter
Rolls Irrespective of the Quiet Period.
The Government claims that systematic citizenship
checks inside the 90-day window “are the only way for
States to ensure that a rush of noncitizens do not illegally
register shortly before a federal election.” U.S. Br. 42–
43. That overlooks checks at registration, which lawfully

27

can be conducted during the quiet period. The NVRA’s
quiet-period provision governs only programs to
“remove the names of ineligible voters from the official
lists of eligible voters.” 52 U.S.C. § 20507(c)(2)(A). It
does not govern review of new applications. Arizon a
already conducts that review. Since 2005, applicants
using the State’s voter registration form have had to
provide documentary proof of citizenship. When a
federal-form applicant does not, the recorder must try to
verify citizenship “[w]ithin ten days after receiving” the
form and must register the applicant as eligible to vote
in only federal elections if the recorder  cannot. Ariz.
Att’y Gen. Op. I25 -007, at 5, 9– 10 ( quoting Ariz. Rev.
Stat. §§  16-121.01(D) –(E), 16-166(F)). Arizona counties
have used SAVE to check registration applicants for
two decades . DHS-AR-551; Burchill, supra , at 1.
The quiet period also leaves recorders free to act on
a specific voter. A State may still remove a particular
noncitizen “on the basis of individualized information,
even within the 90 –day window.” Arcia, 772 F.3d at
1348. This Court has described such “individualized
inquiries” as “permitted under federal law during this
period.” Stay Op. , 2026 WL 2879700, at *3 (emphasis
omitted). What is not permitted is a systematic program
like Arizona’s.
E. Bulk Processing Under Deadline Multiplies the
Risks Associated With  Handling Sensitive
Data.
Finally, the use of SAVE during the quiet period
increases the risk of improperly releasing sensitive data.
Modified SAVE moves a great deal of sensitiv e
information. A single bulk upload may cover “millions of

28

individuals at one time,” Broderick Decl. ¶ 18(b), and
each entry includes a voter’s name, date of birth, and full
or partial Social Security number, League of Women
Voters, 2026 WL 2643439, at *2.  When a partial number
matches, SSA sends DHS the full number in return.
SSA-AR-44. DHS then keeps a record of each case for
ten years. League of Women Voters, 2026 WL 2643439,
at *10. And the States and counties that run the queries
can download the files they uploaded. DHS -AR-1396.
Election offices’ list -maintenance files have been
breached before. In 2023, a Florida county election s
supervisor reported that an unauthorized user appeared
to have copied files “used to conduct voter registration
list maintenance,” exposing the Social S ecurity and
driver’s license numbers of about 58,000 voters. 21
The bulk files are not the only exposure. Correcting
a SAVE error discloses still more sensitive data to
election offices . Texas counties told flagged voters they
could send documentary proof of citizenship by hand,
mail, fax, or email . Nel Decl. ¶ 13. Two declaran ts
emailed images of their passports to county addresses to
keep their registrations. Alex Doe Decl. ¶¶ 13– 14; Cory
Doe Decl. ¶¶ 16, 18. A third, unwilling to send his
passport by email, chose to deliver it in person and
remained unregistered in the meantime. Nel Decl. ¶¶
22–23, 26. According to that declarant, State guidance
directs counties to forward the documents they receiv e
to the secretary of state “to be provided to USCIS.” Id.
¶ 43.

21 C.T. Bowen, Hillsborough  Election Hack Exposed 58,000 Vot ers’
Private Information, Tampa Bay Times  (May 31, 2023) .

29

In the final weeks before an election, the officials
handling this data are also running the election. In
Arizona, t he Yavapai County Recorder reviewed her
SAVE results while preparing for the primary. Burchill,
supra, at 3. The quiet period keeps that work out of the
weeks when officials have the least time to do it
carefully. That serves two of the NVRA’s purposes:
ensuring “accurate and current voter registration rolls”
and implementing the statute “in a manner that
enhances the participation of eligible citizens as voters.”
52 U.S.C. § 20501(b)(2), (4).
CONCLUSION
The Court should hold that the NVRA’s 90 -day
quiet-period provision applies to Arizona ’s program for
canceling registrations based on SAVE results, and it
should affirm the judgment of the court of appeals on the
second question presented.
